claims.text: The coating is an AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy.
The starting coating contains approximately equal fractions of FCC and BCC phases.
The baseline microstructure has relatively coarse, low-density FCC/BCC interphase boundaries.
Rapid quenching and short annealing can produce a high density of coherent FCC/BCC interfaces.
Prolonged high-temperature annealing can produce a coarser distribution of phase boundaries.
TEM, XRD, grain-size, and residual-stress analyses can be used to assess whether interphase-boundary density is decoupled from other heat-treatment-induced changes.
Sustained stresses of approximately 0.5–1.0 GPa at around 700 K promote creep-dominated deformation in this coating.
Nanoscale coherent FCC/BCC interphase boundaries act as effective dislocation-pinning sites.
Under sustained stress and elevated temperature, creep deformation is primarily mediated by dislocation climb and diffusional processes.
Increasing coherent interphase-boundary density interrupts dislocation motion.
Increasing coherent interphase-boundary density raises the activation energy required for dislocation climb.
Impediment of dislocation climb and diffusional creep reduces creep strain.
Relative to the coarse, low-boundary-density baseline, the high-boundary-density samples will have lower creep strain rates.
Relative to the baseline, the high-boundary-density samples will show a delayed onset of accelerated creep and a longer minimum-creep stage.
Higher interphase-boundary density will improve overall creep resistance.
The proposed mechanism is effective over sustained stresses of 0.5–1.0 GPa and temperatures around 700 K.
The proposed operating conditions are typical of protective-coating service environments.
The influence of interphase boundaries may be limited when grain-size changes or secondary-phase formation dominate creep behavior.
